column5: Joseph asks the released cupbearer to remember him
column6: The commentary notes Joseph's request to be remembered and the cupbearer's later forgetting; Genesis gives the request itself, asking the cupbearer to mention him to Pharaoh and bring him out of prison.

column5: Joseph confined in fetters
column6: The commentary places Joseph's waiting in prison; the psalm retells his story as feet bound in fetters until the promised time, giving the confinement a bodily image.

column5: Joseph tested until his word comes true
column6: The commentary arranges Joseph's prison years around delayed remembrance and eventual release; the psalm says the word of the Lord tested Joseph until what he had said came to pass, interpreting the delay as a trial.

column5: Seven years of abundance forecast
column6: The commentary follows Joseph's reading of Pharaoh's dream as a calendar of plenty and scarcity; Genesis predicts seven years of great abundance throughout Egypt, specifying the productive span.

column5: Seven famine years follow
column6: The commentary's Joseph narrative turns from years of yield to years of hardship; Genesis forecasts seven years of famine after the abundance, making the saved grain's time horizon explicit.

column5: The plenty is forgotten in famine
column6: The commentary says the hard years consume what was stored; Genesis adds that the famine is so severe that the former plenty is no longer remembered, a sharper account of yield erased by loss.

column5: The land produces abundantly during the good years
column6: The commentary follows the movement from productive years to preserved grain; Genesis says the land yields abundantly through the seven years, the harvest that makes Joseph's storage possible.

column5: Joseph opens the storehouses in famine
column6: The commentary ends Joseph's cycle with renewed access to produce after scarcity; Genesis says Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain during the famine, showing reserve released when need arrives.

column5: Those who trample the needy
column6: The commentary's garden owners plan to keep the poor from their crop; Amos addresses people who trample the needy and bring the poor to an end, naming the injustice that the garden scene dramatizes.

column5: Poor people traded for silver while wheat is sold
column6: The commentary contrasts hoarded produce with giving; Amos condemns buyers who acquire the poor for silver and sell even wheat refuse, making grain control an instrument of exploitation.

column5: Do not close the hand against the poor
column6: The commentary describes holding a gift back and excluding the poor from a garden; Deuteronomy forbids hardening the heart or shutting the hand against a poor kinsman, a direct ethical counterpoint.

column5: Open the hand to meet another's need
column6: The commentary says squeezing can let its extract flow as generosity; Deuteronomy commands opening the hand and lending enough for the poor person's need, making release the ethical response to scarcity.

column5: Give freely without a grudging heart
column6: The commentary contrasts a generous person with one who withholds or reclaims a gift; Deuteronomy commands giving without regret and promises blessing for the work, joining openhandedness to fruitful outcome.

column5: A forgotten sheaf left for the poor
column6: The commentary's owners plan to keep a garden's entire yield from the poor; Deuteronomy says a forgotten sheaf must remain for the stranger, orphan, and widow, applying release to grain harvest.

column5: Ruth allowed to glean among the sheaves
column6: The commentary's garden owners bar the poor from entering; Boaz tells his workers to let Ruth glean even among the sheaves and not reproach her, reversing exclusion in a concrete harvest scene.

column5: Extra grain deliberately left for Ruth
column6: The commentary treats a crop's extract as a gift that may either flow or be retained; Boaz orders handfuls pulled from the bundles and left for Ruth, making generosity exceed mere permission to glean.

column5: A close relative as guardian and redeemer
column6: The commentary says ancestry and kinship can be a refuge; Naomi identifies Boaz as a near kinsman and redeemer, where family connection becomes practical protection and provision.

column5: The day is short, work is abundant, and the master presses
column6: The commentary calls late afternoon the point when work is nearly done and time for unfinished tasks narrows; this saying makes the same pressure explicit through a short day, much work, and an urgent master.

column5: An oath measures the time until oppression ends
column6: The commentary opens with an oath on time and leaves the promised verdict just beyond the verse; Daniel's angel swears by the living God and gives a measured period whose end coincides with the breaking of the holy people's power.

column5: Blessed is the one who waits to the appointed days
column6: The commentary includes delayed arrival, a fleeting moment, and patience through hard years; Daniel blesses the person who waits and reaches the stated number of days, linking endurance to a measured end.

column5: An oath that there will be no more delay
column6: The commentary hears both a broad age and a late, shortened interval in asr; Revelation's angel swears that there will be no more delay before the mystery is completed, joining oath, waiting, and time's end.

column5: The oath is directed at the disobedient
column6: The commentary places an oath before a verdict of loss; Hebrews continues its reading of Psalm 95 by identifying those excluded from rest as the disobedient, specifying why the sworn exclusion occurs.

column5: Unbelief prevents entry
column6: The commentary moves from a general human loss to an exception for believers; Hebrews says the wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief, giving the faith contrast a precise interpretive role.

column5: The present day is still called Today
column6: The commentary treats a named time as a threshold before action becomes too late; Hebrews says God again appoints a day called Today and warns against hardening the heart, reading the old oath as a present opportunity.

column5: Prayer when heaven is shut and rain withheld
column6: The commentary connects prayer at a set time with clouds, rain, and crop yield; Solomon prays for the people when heaven is closed and there is no rain, linking drought, prayer, repentance, and renewed provision.

column5: Arabic ع ص ر / Hebrew עצר; table sound correspondence, unverified
column6: The package table marks Hebrew עצר as a possible sound correspondence to Arabic ع ص ر; Solomon's prayer describes heaven being shut so rain stops, a relevant restraint of the rain that the commentary links to yield, without proving cognacy.

column5: God is refuge in the cave prayer
column6: The commentary treats a cave as refuge for people whose time is hidden from them; Psalm 142's superscription places David in a cave, and the cited verse calls God his refuge and portion while he is in distress.

column5: Fleeing for refuge and holding fast to hope
column6: The commentary joins seeking shelter with clinging tightly to a person or place; Hebrews describes people who have fled for refuge to seize the hope set before them, bringing refuge and grasping together.

column5: Daniel prays three times each day under threat
column6: The commentary describes believers praying at the day's edges; Daniel continues praying three times daily toward Jerusalem despite a decree that endangers his life, showing fixed prayer times maintained under pressure.

column5: The Lord's Prayer said three times daily
column6: The commentary names the afternoon prayer and describes morning-evening devotion; the Didache directs Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day, evidence of a timed daily discipline.

column5: Cornelius prays at the ninth hour
column6: The commentary leaves open the afternoon-prayer sense of asr; Acts places Cornelius in prayer at the ninth hour when he sees an angel, a distinct Christian scene of late-day devotion.

column5: Evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning
column6: The commentary lets one unqualified time-name span an afternoon, an era, or a fleeting interval; Jesus lists the night watches and warns that the master may come at any one of them, making readiness depend on an unknown hour.

column5: Prayer rises like incense
column6: The commentary describes perfume swelling and rising behind a passing person; the psalm asks that prayer rise like incense, a distinct connection to the commentary's scent image apart from this verse's evening-offering detail.

column5: Wind releases garden spices and fruit
column6: The commentary brings together wind, garden produce, and fragrance carried after movement; the Song calls on the winds to blow through a garden so its spices flow and its fruits can be eaten, joining those images in one scene.

column5: Fragrance set beside the day of death
column6: The commentary follows a woman's perfume trail into a reflection on what remains after someone passes and also makes asr a life's closing time; Ecclesiastes says a good name is better than fragrant oil and the day of death better than birth.

column5: Sow in the morning and keep working in the evening
column6: The commentary says the late day leaves little time for work still undone and connects time with uncertain yield; Ecclesiastes commands sowing in the morning and not letting the hand rest in the evening because the outcome is unknown.

column5: Light darkens as old age approaches
column6: The commentary hears afternoon's fading light alongside the end of a human life; Ecclesiastes depicts sun, light, moon, and stars darkening as the days of aging arrive, giving that decline a bodily and cosmic image.

column5: A life poured out as departure nears
column6: The commentary treats squeezing as extracting a life-giving essence and asr as the close of a lifespan; Paul says he is already being poured out as a libation and that the time of his departure has come.

column5: Transformation in a moment at the last trumpet
column6: The commentary holds long ages beside the instant and says a whole lifetime can shrink to a small part of a day; Paul places the change of the dead in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.

column5: A grain dies and bears much fruit
column6: The commentary describes grain protected in its husk through scarcity and later used for food; Jesus says a grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit, making fruitful release rather than protected storage the condition of abundance.

column5: Harvest comes in due time to those who do not give up
column6: The commentary links the final patience-word to waiting through lean years for stored grain to yield; Paul urges continued good work because harvest comes at the proper time if one does not grow weary.

column5: The tested righteous are refined like gold
column6: The commentary says time's pressure extracts an essence and connects patience with a bitter extract; Wisdom pictures the tested righteous as gold tried in a furnace and accepted like a burnt offering, interpreting pressure as refinement.

column5: A material gift is a fragrant offering
column6: The commentary makes pressed yield an image of generosity and perfume a good trace left behind; Paul calls the Philippians' delivered gift a fragrant offering, joining concrete giving with lingering fragrance.

column5: The fragrance of knowledge spreads everywhere
column6: The commentary describes a scent rising and trailing after movement; Paul says God spreads the fragrance of knowledge through the apostles everywhere, turning a passing procession into a lasting trail.

column5: Aroma received differently by the saved and perishing
column6: The commentary contrasts a good trace left behind with destructive dust and loss; Paul says the same aroma is associated with those being saved and those perishing, adding opposed outcomes to the scent image.

column5: Bitter water becomes drinkable
column6: The commentary's poem imagines water itself as the thing choking the speaker, with no rescuing sip left; at Marah, God shows Moses a tree and the bitter water becomes sweet, a contrasting scene where the obstructing water is made into relief.

column5: The gardener asks for one more year
column6: The commentary's old garden owner loses his final yield when there is no time or strength to plant again; Jesus' gardener asks for another year to dig and fertilize the barren tree, making time an opportunity for restoration.

column5: Rich toward God rather than oneself
column6: The commentary contrasts generous outflow with stored yield kept from others; Jesus concludes that the farmer who stores goods for himself is not rich toward God, giving the accumulation scene its ethical verdict.

column5: A fixed chasm makes relief impossible
column6: The commentary's thirsty speaker has no remaining rescue sip; Abraham says a great chasm is fixed between the two places and no one can cross, explaining why the rich man's requested relief cannot arrive.

column5: Stored wealth decays
column6: The commentary's pressed yield can leave only a dry remainder, and its garden owners lose what they tried to retain; James says riches have rotted and garments are moth-eaten, showing stored wealth failing to preserve its owner.

column5: Corroded treasure testifies in the last days
column6: The commentary joins accumulation and the closing time of a life; James says hoarded gold and silver corrode and become evidence against their owners in the last days, making stored wealth a witness to judgment.

column5: Withheld wages cry out to God
column6: The commentary describes a father withholding a child's property and garden owners denying the poor their produce; James says wages kept back from workers cry out, giving retention a concrete social and judicial consequence.

column5: Luxury before the day of slaughter
column6: The commentary's aging garden owner loses the yield on which his future depends; James depicts the rich living in pleasure and fattening their hearts for a day of slaughter, joining abundance to an approaching end.
